title: Small acts
hookLine: love is mostly in small things

lines: IN THE MORNING, A FULL POT.
cards: Drip. Drip. A leaky faucet over a bucket, or rain off the edge of a roof into a clay pot.
Each drop is almost nothing. Nobody would bother to measure one. Leave the pot there overnight, though, and in the morning it's full to the brim.
A verse in the Dhammapada, an old collection of the Buddha's sayings, uses exactly that picture, and not for water. For goodness. Three traditions speak to how small love can be and still count.

teach.b: First, the water-pot. In Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, the verse warns against thinking lightly of good, as if it could never add up to much.
Then comes the picture: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The wise, it says, become full of good the same way, gathering it little by little.
No single drop fills the pot; every drop is part of the filling. Second, a cup of water.

teach.h: A CUP OF COLD WATER ONLY.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says that whoever gives "a cup of cold water only" to one of his little ones, in the name of a disciple, "shall in no wise lose his reward." Notice the word only. Not a banquet.
Not a fortune. Just water, and cold, which in a hot land is its own kindness. Third, a face.
A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, says in plain words that your smile in the face of your brother is charity.
So, in the same saying, is guiding someone who is lost, or moving a stone out of the road. Charity, here, isn't only money. Fourth, what the three share, each in its own words.
None of them says big acts don't matter.
They say small ones aren't nothing.
A text back. A door held. The dishes done without being asked.
On an ordinary day, love often looks like that, and these teachers say it adds up.

how: Buddhists speak of gathering merit little by little through everyday good deeds, Christians read the cup of cold water as a picture of small service, and the hadith in al-Tirmidhi counts a smile or removing harm from a path among acts of charity.

o: kindnesses too small to measure that add up over time
good deeds that only count when people notice them
gifts of money given to the poor at holy times

games.q: the small things, and where they come from — tap the pairs.
p: a water-pot filled drop by drop
a cup of cold water only
a smile in your brother's face
moving a stone from the road

s: in the hadith, charity means only giving money
the saying counts a smile, guiding the lost and moving a stone from the road.
the Dhammapada compares gathering good to a pot filling with drops
"even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled."
in Matthew, the gift must be a large one to be rewarded
"a cup of cold water only" shall in no wise lose its reward.

games.q: a stranger looks lost in the street, and you have nothing to give but a few seconds. in the saying recorded by al-Tirmidhi, what counts as charity here?
o: nothing, without money it doesn't count.
a smile and showing them the way.
only a prayer for them later.
games.why: the saying counts a smile as charity, and guiding someone who is lost too. the smallest gifts are on the list.

practice: Breathe slowly and let the day ahead come to mind, the places you'll be and the people you'll see, and find three small kindnesses that fit inside it: a glass of water poured for someone, a real smile at the counter, a message that says thinking of you.
See each one clearly, one at a time, the way a drop falls. If you pray, you can offer the day in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Small acts. Kindnesses too small to measure one by one, the drop, the cup of water, the smile, that fill the pot over time. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: small things. Nobody needs to measure the drops for the pot to fill. That's day eight hundred seventy-one.
